title: Sleep duration and cause-specific mortality among US adults with heart disease: A NHIS-NDI linkage cohort study
content:
by Tolulope Victoria Adebile, Tobi Oloyede, Emmanuel Azu, Mobolaji Olagunju, Olamide Asifat, Temitayo Mary Paul, Oluwaseun Ipede, Wandoo Abwa, Purbasha Biswas, Lili Yu

Background

Sleep duration is increasingly recognized as a component of cardiovascular health, yet its prognostic significance among adults with established heart disease remains unclear. We examined associations between sleep duration and mortality among US adults with heart disease.

Methods

We analyzed data from 3,287 adults with heart disease participating in the 2004 National Health Interview Survey linked to the National Death Index through December 31, 2019. Sleep duration was categorized as ≤6 hours, 7–8 hours, and ≥9 hours. Cox proportional hazards models stratified by variables violating the proportional hazards assumption estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all-cause, heart-related, and non-heart-related mortality. Restricted cubic splines evaluated nonlinear dose-response relationships.

Results

During 15 years of follow-up, 49.4% of participants died, including 16.7% from heart-related causes and 32.6% from non-heart-related causes. Compared with 7–8 hours of sleep, long sleep duration (≥9 hours) was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR:1.51 [95% CI:1.32–1.73]), heart-related mortality (HR:1.53 [95% CI:1.22–1.92]), and non-heart-related mortality (HR:1.50 [95% CI:1.27–1.77]). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated nonlinear associations, with the lowest predicted mortality risk occurring at 6–7 hours. Findings remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and age and sex subgroups.

Conclusions

Among US adults with heart disease, long sleep duration was consistently associated with higher risks of all-cause, heart-related, and non-heart-related mortality. Sleep duration may represent a simple marker of residual risk that could enhance risk stratification among adults living with heart disease.
